421.title: The surah without bismillah
421.hook: the only surah that doesn't open with bismillah, which scholars link to its opening in 9:1
421.howItsDone: When reciting surah nine from its beginning, Muslims do not say the bismillah; many begin with a'udhu billah instead, and in printed copies of the Qur'an the surah follows surah eight with no basmala line.

segments.voice: Yesterday: if they incline to peace, and surah eight closed. Your line was incline to peace. Did you take the cup of tea? Today, surah nine, and something missing at its door. Day four hundred twenty-one.
screen: `IF THEY INCLINE TO PEACE — INCLINE TO PEACE.`

segments.voice: Way back on day two of this path, you learned bismillah: in the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Since then you've watched it stand at the top of every surah, a hundred and thirteen times, like a doorway you walk through without looking. Open a printed Qur'an to surah nine, and the doorway isn't there. The page goes straight from the last line of surah eight to the first line of surah nine. Reciters who begin there don't say it. Out of a hundred and fourteen surahs, this is the only one. People have been asking why for fourteen centuries.
screen: `BISMILLAH, A HUNDRED AND THIRTEEN TIMES.` → `SURAH NINE: NO DOORWAY.` → `ASKED FOR FOURTEEN CENTURIES.`

segments.voice: Surah nine has two names. At-Tawbah, Repentance, for the repentance it describes later on. And Bara'ah, from its first word, which means a release, a disavowal, a declared end to obligations. In Pickthall's words, it opens: “Freedom from obligation (is proclaimed) from Allah and His messenger toward those of the idolaters with whom ye made a treaty.” It's a proclamation about treaties that had been broken, read out at the pilgrimage in the ninth year after the emigration. And the verses that follow make an exception: those who kept their treaties are to be honored to the end of their term. Why no bismillah? Scholars give two main explanations. One comes from a report in which the young scholar Ibn Abbas asked the caliph Uthman this very question. Uthman answered that surah eight was among the early Medinan revelations and surah nine among the last, that their content was similar, and that the Prophet ﷺ died without making clear whether nine was part of eight. So the compilers set them side by side and left out the line between them. The second explanation is attributed to Ali: the bismillah is a promise of safety, and this surah opens with that safety withdrawn from treaty-breakers. Many scholars hold both explanations together. And here's a detail people love: the bismillah still appears a hundred and fourteen times in the Qur'an. Surah twenty-seven contains it inside a verse, in a letter from the prophet Sulayman. The count stays whole. Only the doorway here is silent, and the silence itself became something to study.
screen: `BARA'AH — A RELEASE, A DISAVOWAL.` · `TREATIES BROKEN, TREATIES KEPT.` · `UTHMAN'S ANSWER; ALI'S ANSWER.` · `STILL A HUNDRED AND FOURTEEN.` · then, large: `THE SILENCE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think of somewhere in your day where words are usually said, and today notice the gap instead: the greeting a coworker didn't give, the thank-you you skipped, the bismillah you forgot before eating. Don't fix it yet. Just notice that a missing word can say as much as a spoken one. Then pick one place today where you'll say the word, on purpose. The bell holds the time.
The surah without bismillah. At-Tawbah, also called Bara'ah: the one surah that opens without in the name of God, and the reasons scholars give. Today's word.
Your line: the silence speaks. Today, notice one missing word, in your speech or someone else's, and what its absence says. Day four hundred twenty-one.

422.title: The second of two
422.hook: the cave again: the second of two, do not grieve, Allah is with us (9:40)
422.howItsDone: Muslims retell the night in the cave of Thawr with the story of the hijra, honoring the household of Abu Bakr who helped, and some comfort a frightened friend with the verse's words, la tahzan, inna Allaha ma'ana: do not grieve, God is with us.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the surah without bismillah, the one surah that opens with no words of mercy, and your line was the silence speaks. Did something missing say more than words would have? Day four hundred twenty-two.

Late in his life, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ calls for the march to Tabuk, in the worst of the heat. Some people find reasons to stay home. And at-Tawbah, verse thirty-eight, asks them: what's wrong with you, that when you're told to go out, you sink down heavily to the earth? Then, to people dragging their feet, the surah tells a story they all knew. You heard it on this path last year: the cave of Thawr, the night of the hijra, two men hiding while the searchers walked past. Today we come back to the cave, and look at who else was in the story.

Verse forty, in paraphrase: if you don't help him, God already helped him, when he was driven out, the second of two, when the two were in the cave, and he said to his companion, in Pickthall's words: "Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us." Then God sent down His sakina, His calm, on him. On whom? The verse just says him. Some commentators say the Prophet; others say Abu Bakr, the companion told not to grieve. The Arabic allows both, and commentators still discuss it. The verse's point, to the people staying home, is sharp: the Prophet doesn't need you. God helped him when he had one friend. But read the hijra in Bukhari, and the two in the cave weren't quite alone. Abu Bakr's son 'Abdullah came every night after dark, slept near the cave, and slipped back to Mecca before dawn to listen for news. A shepherd, 'Amir ibn Fuhayra, grazed sheep over their tracks and brought them milk. And Abu Bakr's daughter Asma', packing their food for the journey, found nothing to tie the bag with. So she tore her waistband in two and used it to tie up the provisions. She was called dhat an-nitaqayn, she of the two waistbands. The second of two is a phrase about friendship under pressure. Around the two in the cave were people who did small, brave, ordinary things in the dark. A torn belt. A night's walk. A flock driven over footprints.

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone who stayed with you on a bad night: a hospital hallway, a long drive, a phone call that went past midnight. Then the people around that night you hardly thanked: the one who brought food, the one who drove, the one who covered for you at work. Hold them, one by one. If you pray, you can ask good for each of them by name. The bell holds the time.
The second of two. The Qur'an's phrase for the Prophet and his companion hiding in the cave of Thawr, with God as their help. Today's word.
Your line: the second of two. Today, thank one person who helped you through something hard, especially if they did it quietly. Day four hundred twenty-two.

423.title: Friends of one another
423.hook: believing men and women are protectors of one another (9:71)
423.howItsDone: Muslims cite 9:71 when speaking of shared responsibility between men and women in faith and community life; how that cooperation is arranged in mosques, schools and families varies between scholars and communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cave of Thawr and the quiet helpers around it, and your line was the second of two. Who did you thank for helping you through something hard? Day four hundred twenty-three.

Start with grammar. An Arabic plural like "the believers" can cover a mixed group, the way "you all" does. But in some places the Qur'an says it twice: men and women, believing men and believing women. At-Tawbah does it in verse seventy-one, right after a passage about the hypocrites, men and women, who egg each other on toward wrong. Then the surah turns and describes the other kind of community, and gives it a word: awliya'. Friends. Allies. People who stand at each other's side.

Pickthall translates the verse's opening this way: "And the believers, men and women, are protecting friends one of another; they enjoin the right and forbid the wrong". Then it goes on: they keep up the prayer, they pay the zakat, they obey God and His messenger, and God will have mercy on them. Awliya' is the plural of wali. Its root, w-l-y, carries the sense of being near, next to, close enough to turn toward. So a wali is a friend, but also an ally, a guardian, someone who has your back. The same word can describe God's closeness to believers, and in another verse, a guardian in a family. Here it runs sideways, between people. And look at who is in the list. Men and women share every verb: both encourage good, both push back on wrong, both pray, both give. The verse doesn't divide the work and hand half to each. Why name both at all? A report in Ahmad's Musnad gives one answer. Umm Salama, a wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, asked him: why are men mentioned in the Qur'an, and we are not? Later, she heard him reciting from the pulpit a new verse, in Surah al-Ahzab. It names ten qualities, and gives every one of them twice: Muslim men and Muslim women, believing men and believing women, truthful men and truthful women, patient men and women, men and women who give, who fast, who remember God much. For all of them, forgiveness and a great reward. A woman asked a question, and the answer came back spelled out ten times over. Scholars disagree about many details of how men and women work together. This verse is a common starting point: protectors of each other.
screen: `MEN AND WOMEN, PROTECTING FRIENDS.` · `W-L-Y — NEAR, AT YOUR SIDE.` · `THE SAME VERBS FOR BOTH.` · `UMM SALAMA ASKS; TEN PAIRS COME.` · then, large: `PROTECTORS OF EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of someone of the other sex in your life: a sister, a brother, a colleague, a classmate, a neighbor. Is there a place where their good idea went unheard, or their work got credited to someone else? Picture yourself doing what the verse describes: standing at their side, speaking up for the right thing, simply and decently. If you pray, you can ask for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Awliya'. Friends, allies, protectors, from a root that means to be near. Believing men and women, at each other's side. Today's word.
Your line: protectors of each other. Today, in one meeting, chat or conversation, make sure one person's good point gets heard and credited to them. Day four hundred twenty-three.

424.title: A mosque founded on piety
424.hook: a mosque founded on mindfulness from the first day, with people who love to be clean (9:108)
424.howItsDone: Visitors to Medina pray at the Quba mosque, some after making wudu first, following the hadith on its reward; volunteers in mosques around the world take turns cleaning the prayer hall and the washing area.

segments.voice: Yesterday, awliya', believing men and women at each other's side, and your line was protectors of each other. Whose good point did you make sure got heard? Day four hundred twenty-four.

Two buildings on the edge of Medina, both with a place to pray, both facing the same direction. From the street, you might not tell them apart. One was built, the Qur'an says, to cause harm, to split the believers and to give cover to someone working against them. The other was built on something you can't see in the brickwork at all. At-Tawbah tells the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ never to stand in the first one. And it points to the second, with a phrase about foundations that people have carried ever since.
screen: `ONE BUILT ON WHAT YOU CAN'T SEE.`

segments.voice: Verse one hundred seven describes a mosque set up to do damage and to divide; tradition calls it Masjid ad-Dirar, the mosque of harm. Verse one hundred eight says, in paraphrase: never stand in it. A mosque founded on taqwa from the first day is more worthy for you to stand in. In it are people who love to purify themselves, and God loves those who purify themselves. Taqwa is the word Pickthall renders here as duty to Allah, and others as piety or mindfulness: a constant awareness of God that shapes what you do. So a building can have a foundation under the foundation. Which mosque is meant? Some commentators say Quba, the mosque built when the Prophet reached the edge of Medina, just after the journey that began in the cave. A hadith in Muslim's collection has the Prophet naming his own mosque in Medina. Scholars have held both, and some say the verse fits both. Then the cleanliness. Commentators connect the people who love to purify themselves with the people of Quba, who were known for washing carefully with water. A hadith reported by Ibn Majah and an-Nasa'i says that whoever purifies himself at home, then comes to Quba and prays there, has a reward like a lesser pilgrimage. Inner and outer meet in one verse: a heart that's honest about why it built something, and hands that keep the place clean. Neither is an extra. The intention is the foundation; the cleaning is how you live in the house.
screen: `THE MOSQUE OF HARM.` · `TAQWA FROM THE FIRST DAY.` · `QUBA, OR THE PROPHET'S MOSQUE.` · `PEOPLE WHO LOVE TO BE CLEAN.` · then, large: `FOUNDED ON PIETY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of a place you share with other people. A kitchen, an office, a break room, a prayer room, a stairwell. Picture the corner of it nobody takes care of. Ask yourself one quiet question, the verse's question: why do I do the things I do there? When the bell ends, you can go and clean that one corner, without telling anyone. If you pray, you can begin it with bismillah. The bell holds the time.
A mosque founded on piety. A place built from the first day on taqwa, awareness of God, and kept by people who love to be clean. Today's word.
screen: `A MOSQUE FOUNDED ON PIETY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: founded on piety. Today, before you start one thing, a project, a message, a plan, check the foundation: why am I building this? Day four hundred twenty-four.

425.title: The three left behind
425.hook: three men who stayed from Tabuk are forgiven after long waiting because they told the truth (9:118)
425.carry: the earth felt narrow, then wide
425.howItsDone: The story of Ka'b ibn Malik is taught at length in Muslim study circles as a lesson in honesty and repentance, and 9:118–119 are recited as a reminder that God turns toward people so that they can turn back, and to be with the truthful.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a mosque founded on piety, built on taqwa from the first day. Your line was founded on piety. When you checked why you were building something, what did you find? Day four hundred twenty-five.

Dawn, in Medina. A man is praying the morning prayer on the roof of his house, alone. For fifty nights, no one in the city has spoken to him. Then, from the top of a hill called Sal', a voice shouts, as loud as it can: Ka'b ibn Malik, good news! He falls down in prostration. You met Ka'b last year, on the day he told the Prophet ﷺ the plain truth: he had no excuse for staying home from Tabuk. Today we read the verse that ended his waiting, and what the waiting was like from the inside.

Ka'b tells the waiting himself, in Bukhari and Muslim. His two companions in it, Murara and Hilal, stayed home and wept. Ka'b, the youngest, kept going out. He prayed in the mosque, greeted the Prophet, and watched to see if his lips moved in reply. Then a letter came from the north, from the king of Ghassan: we hear your master has shunned you; come to us, and we'll honor you. Ka'b read it and said: this too is a test. And he threw it into an oven. An open door to comfort, and he burned it. Then verse one hundred eighteen came down. In paraphrase: God turned also to the three who were left behind, when the earth, vast as it is, became narrow for them, and their own souls became narrow, and they knew there was no refuge from God except in Him. Then He turned to them, so that they could turn. Notice the order. God turns first; then they turn. The verse before it, one hundred seventeen, says God had already turned to the Prophet and to those who marched with him in the hour of hardship, after some of their hearts had nearly swerved. So the three aren't set apart as the only ones who needed mercy. They're placed in the same sentence as everyone who went. And verse one hundred nineteen closes it: be with the truthful. When Ka'b came to the Prophet that morning, it was the Prophet's face that was shining with joy. Ka'b offered to give away all his wealth; he was told to keep some. And he vowed that, since the truth had saved him, he would speak only the truth for the rest of his life.
screen: `A KING'S LETTER, INTO THE OVEN.` · `THE EARTH, VAST, GREW NARROW.` · `GOD TURNS FIRST; THEN THEY TURN.` · `BE WITH THE TRUTHFUL.` · then, large: `THE EARTH FELT NARROW, THEN WIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait honestly for forgiveness. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind something you got wrong, where you're still waiting: for someone to answer, to soften, to trust you again. Notice the narrowness of it. Notice, too, any easy way out that's being offered, a story that would make it not your fault. Don't take it. Just wait, honestly, for these two minutes. If you pray, you can turn toward God with it, the way the three did, with nowhere else to go. The bell holds the time.
The three left behind. Ka'b, Murara and Hilal, who told the truth about Tabuk, waited fifty nights, and were turned to by God in 9:118. Today's word.
Your line: the earth felt narrow, then wide. Today, if something offers you an easy way out of an honest wait, notice it, and leave it in the oven. Day four hundred twenty-five.

426.title: Grieved by your suffering
426.hook: a messenger from among you, grieved by your suffering, kind and merciful (9:128)
426.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the last two verses of at-Tawbah as part of their daily remembrance, and send blessings on the Prophet, sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam, each time his name is mentioned.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three left behind, who told the truth and waited fifty nights. Your line was the earth felt narrow, then wide. Did an easy way out tempt you, and did you leave it in the oven? Day four hundred twenty-six.

A month ago, with 'Isa's answer at the end of al-Ma'idah, you heard in passing that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once wept over that verse. Here is the whole report, from Muslim's collection. He was reciting, and came to verses where Ibrahim speaks to God about his people, and then 'Isa does the same. He raised his hands and said: my community, my community. And he wept. God sent Jibril to ask him why he was weeping, though God already knew. And the answer came back: We will please you concerning your community, and We will not grieve you. Near the very end of at-Tawbah, there's a verse that describes the man who wept.

Verse one hundred twenty-eight, in paraphrase: there has come to you a messenger from among yourselves. Whatever burdens you weighs heavy on him. He is deeply concerned for you, and to the believers he is kind and merciful. Take it a phrase at a time. From among yourselves: not a stranger, not an angel, a man who grew up in their streets. Then: 'azizun 'alayhi ma 'anittum. What you suffer is hard on him. Your trouble becomes his trouble. Then: harisun 'alaykum, eager for you, anxious that things go well for you. A hadith in Bukhari gives a picture of that anxiety. The Prophet said: my likeness and yours is like a man who lit a fire, and moths and insects keep flying into it, and I'm holding you by your belts, pulling you back from the flames. And then two words: ra'uf, rahim, kind and merciful. Commentators point out something remarkable here. Ar-Ra'uf and ar-Rahim are both names of God. In this one verse, the Qur'an gives them to the Prophet as qualities, without making him more than a man. Notice, too, the direction of the verse. It doesn't tell anyone to feel for the Prophet. It says he already feels for you. This is the second-to-last verse of a surah full of armies, excuses and hard warnings, and it ends with a portrait of tenderness. Whatever you're carrying today, the portrait says, someone carried the worry of it long before you arrived.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel for someone's trouble. Sit, and breathe slowly. Think of one person who is struggling right now. Don't solve it. Just let their trouble be hard on you for a moment, the way the verse describes. What are they carrying? What does it feel like to carry it? Stay with them for a few breaths. If you pray, you can send peace and blessings on the Prophet, the way many Muslims do whenever his name is said, or ask for the person by name. The bell holds the time.
Grieved by your suffering. The Qur'an's portrait of the Prophet in 9:128: your hardship is hard on him, he is eager for your good, kind and merciful. Today's word.
Your line: he felt it with you. Today, when someone tells you about a problem, let the first thing you say show you felt it, before you say anything useful. Day four hundred twenty-six.

427.title: Enough for me
427.hook: Allah is enough for me, in Him I trust, Lord of the Throne (9:129)
427.tomorrow: Block A close: the long surahs
427.howItsDone: Some Muslims recite 9:129, hasbiya Allahu la ilaha illa huwa, seven times morning and evening as part of their daily remembrance, and say hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil in moments of fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a messenger grieved by your suffering, kind and merciful. Your line was he felt it with you. When someone told you a problem, what did you say first? Day four hundred twenty-seven, the end of a week.

This week, at-Tawbah. It opened with no bismillah, a silence at the door. It took us into a cave with the second of two. It called believing men and women protectors of each other. It set two mosques side by side and asked what's under the bricks. It sat with three men in fifty nights of silence, and then painted a portrait of a messenger who feels your trouble as his own. Now the surah's very last verse. After all that, the battles, the excuses, the hypocrites, the forgiveness, it ends on a line a person can say at three in the morning.

Verse one hundred twenty-nine begins: and if they turn away. It imagines the worst outcome, people rejecting everything the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has brought. And it tells him what to say. In Pickthall's translation: "Allah sufficeth me. There is no God save Him. In Him have I put my trust, and He is Lord of the Tremendous Throne." In Arabic, it starts hasbiya Allah. Hasb means enough, a sufficiency. Hasbiya: my enough. God is my enough. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say they won't turn away. It doesn't promise the plan works. It says: even if it doesn't, I'm not empty-handed. Then three steps. No god but Him, so nothing else gets that place. In Him I trust: tawakkul, leaning your whole weight. And the Throne, the Qur'an's picture of God's rule over everything. The same root runs through another phrase you may hear: hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil, God is enough for us, and the best one to rely on. Bukhari reports that Ibrahim said it when he was thrown into the fire, and the Prophet and his companions said it when they were told an army had gathered against them. Some Muslims say today's verse seven times, morning and evening, following a report in Abu Dawud that whoever does so, God will be enough for whatever worries him. A long, hard surah, full of armies and excuses, ends on one person, alone, saying: enough.
screen: `AND IF THEY TURN AWAY.` · `HASBIYA ALLAH — GOD IS MY ENOUGH.` · `NO GOD BUT HIM. IN HIM I TRUST.` · `IBRAHIM IN THE FIRE.` · then, large: `ALLAH IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say hasbiyallah in worry. Sit, and breathe. Let one real worry come up, the one that's been waiting in the back of your mind. Look at it. Then, if you pray, you can say the verse's words quietly, hasbiya Allah, God is enough for me, and let the breath out slowly after them. If you don't, you can simply notice the weight of the worry and set it down beside you for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Enough for me. Hasbiya Allah, the last verse of at-Tawbah: even if they turn away, God is enough, and in Him I trust. Today's word.
Your line: allah is enough. Today, the next time a worry tightens your chest, pause before you check your phone, and let the line come first. Day four hundred twenty-seven.

original.note: Arabic: "God is enough for me," the opening of 9:129, from hasb, a sufficiency.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calming phrase.
what it means: even if everything fails, God is enough, so trust has somewhere to rest.
what a scholar hears: 9:129 closes the surah after 9:128; Abu Dawud reports the sevenfold morning and evening recitation, and the phrase echoes 3:173, hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil.
